rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative pronoun الذين is most eloquently declined with yāʾ in all three cases, though some Arabs use wāw in the nominative; dropping its nūn is permitted, though some restrict that to poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: والأفصح كونه بالياء في أحواله الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians disagree about how الذين is recognized; unlike الذي, it is restricted to rational beings.
rows.anchor: ويخص العقلاء بخلاف الذي ،   فإنه ينطلق على ذي العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Niʿma denotes ease and softness of living; the south wind and ostrich are also named from softness, and anʿama ʿalayhi means to bestow abundantly.
rows.anchor: لين العيش وخفضه ،   ولذلك قيل للجنوب النعامي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anʿama is one of twenty-four functions of the form أفعل: it makes someone possess the base noun, while implying benefaction and taking على instead of its original direct object.
rows.anchor: أنعمته أي جعلته صاحب نعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attached tāʾ is the second-person masculine singular pronoun; أنت consists of two pronouns and is a compound.
rows.anchor: التاء المتصلة بأنعم ضمير المخاطب المذكر المفرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians treat على as a preposition; Sībawayh and a group of later Basran grammarians treat it as a ظرف noun except in certain constructions. It can express literal or figurative elevation and several other relations.
rows.anchor: حرف جر عند الأكثرين ،   إلا إذا جرت بمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suffix هم is a masculine plural pronoun referring to rational absent people, and it can occupy nominative, accusative, or genitive position.
rows.anchor: هم ضمير جمع غائب مذكر عاقل ،   ويكون في موضع رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten reported pronunciations vary the hāʾ and mīm between ḍamma and kasra, mīm sukūn or vowel, and a following yāʾ or wāw: Hamza, the majority, al-Hasan, Ibn Kathīr, Qālūn, al-Aʿraj, and al-Khaffāf are among those named; Ibn Mujāhid adds ʿUmar b. Fāʾid, and ʿAmr b. Fāʾid is also cited.
rows.anchor: وإسكان الميم ،   وهي قراءة حمزة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali identifies the straight path as the Qurʾān; Ibn ʿAbbās is also cited for this interpretation.
rows.anchor: الصراط القرآن ،   قاله علي وابن عباس

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī says a report from the Prophet explains the path as God's Book or faith and its concomitants, Islam and its laws, or the moderate way.
rows.anchor: ذكر المهدوي أنه روي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو العالية والحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya and al-Hasan identify the path as the way of the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وعمر ،   قاله أبو العالية والحسن

rows.speaker: فضيل بن عياض
rows.claim: Fudayl b. ʿIyāḍ interprets the straight path as the way of pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: طريق الحج ،   قاله فضيل بن عياض

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: ʿUthmān interprets the straight path as the Sunan.
rows.anchor: أو السنن ،   قاله عثمان ،   أو طريق الجنة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr interprets the straight path as the way to Paradise.
rows.anchor: أو طريق الجنة ،   قاله سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī interprets the straight path as the way of Sunna and the community.
rows.anchor: أو طريق السنة والجماعة ،   قاله القشيري

rows.speaker: الترمذي
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhī interprets the straight path as the way of fear and hope.
rows.anchor: أو طريق الخوف والرجاء ،   قاله الترمذي ،   أو جسر

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd interprets the straight path as the bridge over Hell.
rows.anchor: أو جسر جهنم ،   قاله عمرو بن عبيد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One Sufi reading asks for guidance through becoming absent from the path, so that one is not bound to the path; Abū Ḥayyān says such readings do not follow the wording, while acknowledging their experiential insight.
rows.anchor: قول بعضهم : { اهدنا الصراط المستقيم } بالغيبوبة عن الصراط لئلا يكون مربوطا بالصراط

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Al-Junayd says asking for guidance amid bewilderment is among the clearest pre-eternal attributes; the request seeks the qualities of servanthood to avoid absorption in those attributes.
rows.anchor: قول الجنيد أن سؤال الهداية عند الحيرة من أشهار الصفات

rows.speaker: الفخر الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects identifying the path as the Qurʾān or Islam and its laws because those favored people supposedly lived before the Qurʾān and this Islamic dispensation.
rows.anchor: رد الفخر الرازي على من قال إن الصراط المستقيم هو القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says al-Rāzī's objection works only if the favored people are proved to be pre-Islamic; the source will report differing identifications of them, so that premise is unsettled.
rows.anchor: وهذا الرد لا يتأتى له إلا إذا صح أن الذين أنعم الله عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request for guidance follows naturally from the preceding declaration of worship and reliance: worship is sound only through guidance to the clear route that reaches its goal.
rows.anchor: لما أخبر المتكلم أنه هو ومن معه يعبدون الله ويستعينونه

rows.speaker: الحسن والضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Dahhāk read صراطاً مستقيماً without the definite article; صراط الذين then apposes a definite expression to an indefinite one, as in 42:52.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ،   والضحاك : صراطا مستقيما دون تعريف

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq reads صراط مستقيم with an annexation, meaning the upright religion; with this and the majority reading, صراط الذين is a clarifying apposition of one definite expression to another.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر الصادق : صراط مستقيم بالإضافة ،   أي الدين المستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apposition identifies the somewhat ambiguous previously mentioned straight path, repeats the request for emphasis, and directs it to the route of those favored.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر قبل { اهدنا الصراط المستقيم } كان فيه بعض إبهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rare alternative says the second path is different from the first, as if a conjunction had been read between them; the commentators disagree about what this second path denotes.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب القول أن الصراط الثاني ليس الأول ،   بل هو غيره

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad says the path is knowledge of God and understanding Him.
rows.anchor: العلم بالله والفهم عنه ،   قاله جعفر بن محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations identify the path as observing the obligations and following the Sunan, or as inward agreement with outward practice in the completion of blessing.
rows.anchor: قيل التزام الفرائض واتباع السنن ،   وقيل هو موافقة الباطن للظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation of inward and outward blessing is linked to 31:20, which says God has poured out both manifest and hidden blessings upon you.
rows.anchor: قال تعالى : { وأسبغ عليكم نعمه ظاهرة وباطنة }

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وعمر وابن الزبير وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Zayd b. ʿAlī read صراط من أنعمت عليهم.
rows.anchor: صراط من أنعمت عليهم ،   ابن مسعود ،   وعمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among the proposed referents of those favored are prophets, angels, and the unaltered communities of Moses and Jesus; Abū Ḥayyān lists these as alternatives rather than restricting the wording to one group.
rows.anchor: والمنعم عليهم هنا الأنبياء أو الملائكة أو أمة موسى وعيسى الذين لم يغيروا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is cited for identifying those favored as believers.
rows.anchor: المؤمنون ،   قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عطية عن ابن عباس والجمهور
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority mean the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, deriving this from 4:69.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : والجمهور أراد صراط النبيين والصديقين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan identifies those favored as the Companions of the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group identifies those favored as the believers among the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة : مؤمنو بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses' followers before they changed their religion.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : أصحاب موسى قبل أن يبدلوا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda limits those favored to the prophets.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : الأنبياء خاصة

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya identifies those favored as Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية : محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبو بكر وعمر

rows.speaker: وكيع
rows.claim: Wakīʿ identifies those favored as Muslims.
rows.anchor: المسلمون ،   قاله وكيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording leaves the blessing unrestricted, so it can encompass every kind of blessing through a general use of the category.
rows.anchor: ولم يقيد الأنعام ليعم جميع الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proposed explanations of God's favor include creating people for felicity, rescuing them from destruction, and guiding them to follow the Messenger; the wording itself does not specify a restriction.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنعم عليهم بخلقهم للسعادة ،   وقيل بأن نجاهم من الهلكة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila affirm that God bestows blessing on unbelievers, while other theologians deny it.
rows.anchor: فأثبتها المعتزلة ونفاها غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional phrase عليهم is in the accusative position because it is governed by an active verb; the same applies to a preposition governed by a non-passive verb or equivalent.
rows.anchor: وموضع عليهم نصب ،   وكذا كل حرف جر تعلق بفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active attribution of favor appeals for acceptance of the request: since God has already favored them, answering their plea for guidance is consistent with His beneficence.
rows.anchor: وبناء أنعمت للفاعل استعطاف لقبول التوسل بالدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer asks that guidance to the path of the favored continue: those who praise God and declare worship and reliance already possess guidance, but ask for its permanence.
rows.anchor: ومضمون هذه الجملة طلب استمرار الهداية إلى طريق من أنعم الله عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr is always masculine singular; it expresses difference in some respect, originates as an adjective, can mark exception, and remains annexed. It cannot take al and does not ordinarily become definite by annexation.
rows.anchor: مفرد مذكر دائما وإذا أريد به المؤنث جاز تذكير الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrāj says ghayr becomes definite when its complement is one specified entity; Sībawayh allows a non-pure annexation to become definite by intent. The commentators also discuss its fronting in predication.
rows.anchor: ومذهب ابن السراج أنه إذا كان المغاير واحدا تعرف بإضافته إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In predication, ghayr or mithl tends to precede its complement; the cited line means the speaker is unlike people who are deceived, and reversed order would distort the point.
rows.anchor: غرضه أنه ليس ممن ينخدع ويغتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anger is a change in disposition caused by something disliked; it can also mean turning away, since turning away is one consequence of anger.
rows.anchor: تغير الطبع لمكروه ،   وقد يطلق على الإعراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā can be a particle of negation, prohibition, or augmentation; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the Kufan view that it can be a noun.
rows.anchor: حرف يكون للنفي وللطلب وزائدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍalāl can mean ruin, concealment, loss, ignorance of an object's location, waste, neglect, forgetting, departure from the proper route, bewilderment, or hesitation; Qurʾanic usage also includes lack of detailed knowledge and love.
rows.anchor: والضلال : الهلاك ،   والخفاء ضل اللبن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read ghayr in the genitive; al-Khalīl reports Ibn Kathīr's accusative reading, also attributed to ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.
rows.anchor: روى الخليل عن ابن كثير النصب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī parses genitive ghayr as an apposition either to الذين or to the pronoun in عليهم; Abū Ḥayyān calls both analyses weak because apposition by an adjective is weak.
rows.anchor: على البدل من الذين ،   عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh parses genitive ghayr as an adjective, treating it as definite through annexation to عليهم; Ibn al-Sarrāj offers a different account of its definiteness.
rows.anchor: على النعت عن سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that الذين denotes a generic class, allowing ghayr to modify it despite definiteness, undermines the rule that a definite noun is modified only by a definite; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this account.
rows.anchor: ولا أختار هذا المذهب وتقرير فساده في النحو

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī and others parse accusative ghayr as a circumstantial accusative from عليهم, or from الذين; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the latter because the genitive complement has no syntactic position for a circumstantial modifier.
rows.anchor: من الذين قاله المهدوي وغيره

rows.speaker: الأخفش والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj allow accusative ghayr as a disconnected exception because the preceding wording does not include those who are astray; some readers reject this analysis because of lā.
rows.anchor: على الاستثناء ،   قاله الأخفش ،   والزجاج وغيرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some permit accusative ghayr as an exception by treating lā as extra, since they say lā is extra only after prior negation; they cite Qurʾanic and poetic examples, while other grammarians take lā as genuinely negative.
rows.anchor: ومن ذهب إلى الاستثناء جعل لا صلة ،   أي زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the alleged proof that lā is extra in the verse of the generous man is not decisive: lā itself is the object of أبى, and البخل is its apposition or a causal object.
rows.anchor: ولا دليل في ذلك ،   بل الأظهر أن لا مفعول بأبى

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: An alternative analysis, attributed to al-Khalīl, treats ghayr as an accusative with an implicit أعني, 'I mean'.
rows.anchor: انتصب غير بإضمار أعني وعزي إلى الخليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase عليهم is in the nominative position as the passive verb's deputy subject; grammarians dispute whether a prepositional phrase can occupy that role.
rows.anchor: وعليهم في موضع رفع بالمغضوب على أنه مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā reinforces the negation already contained in ghayr and is attached to المغضوب عليهم to avoid suggesting that الضالين is coordinated with الذين.
rows.anchor: لتأكيد معنى النفي ،   لأن غير فيه النفي

rows.speaker: عمر وأبي
rows.claim: ʿUmar and Ubayy read غير الضالين, with reports of both accusative and genitive on the rāʾ in the two occurrences; Abū Ḥayyān says the reading marks the angered and astray as distinct, while lā is the likelier emphasis.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر وأبي وغير الضالين ،   وروي عنهما في الراء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī uses the alleged parallel between ghayr and lā to allow a governed object before ghayr; Abū Ḥayyān calls the argument very weak, since similarity of meaning does not transfer syntax without Arabic attestation.
rows.anchor: وأوردها الزمخشري على أنها مسألة مقررة مفروغ منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some supply an omitted صراط before ghayr; Abū Ḥayyān finds the estimate weak because it creates awkward apposition or adjective order and other difficult attachment analyses.
rows.anchor: قال التقدير غير صراط المغضوب عليهم

rows.speaker: أيوب السختياني
rows.claim: Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads ولا الضألين, turning the alif into hamza to avoid two adjacent sukūns; Abū Ḥayyān says the sound change is not productive, though Abū Zayd and Abū al-Fatḥ attest it as a dialect and cite Arab usage and poetry.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أيوب السختياني : ولا الضألين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause of الذين uses a past verb to make God's favor definite and established; the clause with أل uses a participle encompassing all times, and makes the anger passive rather than directly ascribing it to God.
rows.anchor: وجعل الإنعام في صلة الذين ،   والغضب في صلة أل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance.
rows.anchor: وبناه للمفعول ،   لأن من طلب منه الهداية ونسب الأنعام إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing intended is religious; those angered and those astray are general categories covering everyone who incurs anger or goes astray.
rows.anchor: في كل من غضب عليه وضل

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن مسعود ،   وابن عباس ،   ومجاهد ،   والسدي ،   وابن زيد

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم عن رسول الله
rows.claim: The Jews-and-Christians identification is also related from ʿAdī b. Ḥātim from the Prophet; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be adopted if the report is sound.
rows.anchor: عن عدي بن حاتم ،   عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported identification makes those angered the Jews and those astray the polytheists; Abū Ḥayyān notes other views without specifying them here.
rows.anchor: وقيل اليهود والمشركون ،   وقيل غير ذلك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A Sufi restriction interprets those angered as people who neglect proper courtesy while serving God, and the astray as those who perceive that conduct; Abū Ḥayyān says the wording does not support such restrictions.
rows.anchor: كقول بعضهم غير المغضوب عليهم ،   بترك حسن الأدب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's anger may mean His intent to requite a sinner, making it an attribute of essence because His knowledge precedes creation and sin; alternatively it is imposing punishment, an attribute of action.
rows.anchor: والغضب من الله تعالى إرادة الانتقام من العاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anger precedes misguidance in the wording although it results from it because it contrasts with favor: favor brings good and requital brings harm; the order also suits the sūra's cadence.
rows.anchor: وقدم الغضب على الضلال ،   وإن كان الغضب من نتيجة الضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunctive wāw does not itself establish temporal priority; if Jews and Christians are intended, the order may reflect chronology or the Jews' greater hostility, as they came earlier.
rows.anchor: وكان العطف بالواو الجامعة التي لا دلالة فيها على التقديم والتأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra's closing phrases are an instance of parallel cadence (sajʿ mutawāzī), with the final words matching in meter and rhyme; the author also lists specification, apposition, and word order among its rhetorical features.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه السورة من التسجيع المتوازي ،   وهو اتفاق الكلمتين الأخيرتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān concludes that the sūra is seven verses by consensus apart from disregarded dissent; Meccan and Kufan counters differ over whether the basmala or صراط الذين is an āya, while ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd counts eight and Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī six.
rows.anchor: والإجماع على أنها سبع آيات إلا ما شذ فيه من لا يعتبر خلافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the basmala at each sūra's opening is not an āya, while Ibn al-Mubārak anomalously counted it as an āya in every sūra; Abū Ḥayyān says he does not know the principle behind determining āya length.
rows.anchor: ولم يختلفوا في أن البسملة في أول كل سورة ليست آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports about the sūra's letter count, supposed occasions of revelation, basmala's merit, and many titles are not necessarily causes of revelation or core tafsīr; only sound Prophetic clarification, occasions, and abrogation are indispensable to tafsīr.
rows.anchor: وذكروا سبب نزولها ما لا يعد سبب نزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word Āmīn is not Qurʾān; Abū Ḥayyān omits discussion of its forms, meaning, and prayer ruling, along with introductory istiʿādha, as material outside his intended tafsīr scope.
rows.anchor: وليست من القرآن ،   فلذلك أضربنا عن الكلام عليها صفحا
